clarity.justification: The hypothesis makes a clear directional prediction—“high early,” “minimal in the middle,” and “rising again late”—and the proposed layerwise probes and interventions directly address whether a shared-computation window exists. It is falsifiable because failure to observe the predicted U-shaped language-ID curve, inverse content-decoding relationship, or intervention success that “peak[s] at trough” would contradict it, although no numeric decision thresholds are supplied. Important specifications remain ambiguous, especially how “content decodability” is operationalized, how activations are pooled across tokens, and what constitutes cross-lingual patching or concept-editing success; the claim itself acknowledges that “Content decodability is hard to define independently of language.”

feasibility.justification: Activation extraction, layerwise probing, shuffled-label controls, and curve comparisons in “Extract activations for parallel multilingual text across all layers” are standard operations supported by established deep-learning and interpretability tooling, and multilingual models and parallel corpora exist, though no specific model, dataset, sample size, model scale, or other concrete resource figure is named. The hardest step is “cross-lingual patching and concept editing success by layer”; these intervention families are implementable, but the proposal leaves activation alignment, patch targets, editing procedure, and success metric undefined, requiring substantial custom design rather than merely routine execution. The refuting branch is runnable in broad form because layerwise comparisons, “shuffled labels,” and the stated “monolingual model” control can yield negative results, but those controls do not fully resolve probe-capacity confounding or define a language-independent content baseline.
